1The addition rule for counting

Rule The Addition Rule

If activity can be done in ways and activity can be done in ways, then the number of ways you can do exactly one of these activities is .

This extends to groups of many activities.

Example

In a small town, there are only two places where you can buy a new pair of shoes.

In the first location, there are 5 pairs of shoes that fit you.

In the second location, there are 11 pairs of shoes that fit you.

If you want to buy one pair of shoes in this town that fit you, how many ways can you do this?

: buy a pair of shoes that fit from the first location.  

: buy a pair of shoes that fit from the second location.  

The number of ways to perform exactly one of and is .

✎ Explanation (added)

Two counting rules now, and the wording tells you which one applies. “Do one or the other” (exactly one activity): add. “Do one and then the other” (a sequence): multiply, as in last lecture’s soup-and-sandwich example. Buying one pair from shop 1 or shop 2 gives . Buying one pair from each shop would be . The addition rule needs the two activities to have no way in common, which is true here because a pair of shoes is in only one shop.

Textbook · Devore — Devore’s §2.3 (pp. 66–72) builds everything from the product rule; the addition rule for counting is not stated as a separate result there.

2Example: counting paths in a tree

Example

How many paths are there from the top of the tree to the indicated node or leaf at the bottom of the tree.

You can only move down and to the left, or down and to the right.

To make a path to any given node, we will first make a path to one of the nodes above it.

The number [of] paths we can make to this node is .

Answer: 6.

Try it — trace the paths one at a time

Pick a leaf on the bottom row and step through every path that reaches it.

Interactive widget: open the page on a screen to use it.
✎ Explanation (added)

This is the addition rule in action. To arrive at a node you must come from exactly one of the (at most two) nodes directly above it, so the count at a node is the sum of the counts above it. Working down: row 1 is ; row 2 is ; row 3 is ; row 4 is . The marked leaf is .

Look ahead: to reach the middle leaf you take 4 steps, 2 of them to the left. Choosing which 2 of the 4 steps go left is a combination, , the formula from later in this lecture.

3Example: 7-digit phone numbers with no repeated digits

Example

How many 7 digit phone numbers are there with no repeated digits?

Let’s come up with a sequence of activities that can be used to generate these numbers.

: Choose the first digit.← can’t be a zero or a one.
: Choose the second digit.← can’t be what we chose earlier.
: Choose the third digit.← can’t be the same as the 1st or 2nd digit.
⋮
: Choose the 7th digit.

Note that every number we care about can be generated using this process, and different choices lead to different numbers.

The number of ways to perform this sequence of activities is equal to the number of 7 digit phone numbers with no repeated digits.

Number of 7 digit phone numbers with no repeated digits is

(multiplication rule)

✎ Explanation (added)

Where each number comes from. There are 10 digits, 0 to 9. First digit: not 0 and not 1, leaving 8. Second digit: any of the 10 except the one already used, leaving 9 (0 and 1 are allowed again here). Third digit: any except the two already used, 8. Then 7, 6, 5, 4.

Why multiplying is legal even though the available digits change: the multiplication rule only needs the number of choices at each step to be the same no matter what was chosen before. Whatever the first digit was, exactly 9 digits remain for the second. Arithmetic check: , , , , , .

Textbook · Devore — the product rule for k-tuples (a sequence of k choices): §2.3, pp. 68–69, Examples 2.19 and 2.20.

4Example: arranging interviews

Example

Acme Stats Inc is hiring and has short listed the following candidates:

Marian, Jane, Jill, Nicole,   ← Women
Mark, Bob, Jack   ← Men.

How many ways can the interviews be arranged if all the women are interviewed before the men?

Activity : Interview the 4 women.    Activity : Interview the 3 men.

The number of ways to perform and then is

✎ Explanation (added)

The first interview can be any of the 4 women, the second any of the remaining 3, and so on: orders for the women. Then orders for the men. Every order of the women can be followed by every order of the men, so multiply: . The “!” (factorial) notation is introduced formally with permutations below.

Example Follow-up

If the order of the interviews is chosen at random and all orderings are equally likely to be chosen, what is the probability all women are interviewed before the men?

Classical case ⟹

Typed note included in the PDF Aran’s typed notes

Ask towards the end of the course if this is likely or not

0.02857 is very unlikely

✎ Explanation (added)

“All orderings equally likely” puts us in the classical case, , so the whole problem is two counts. The top was just found: 144. The bottom is every possible order of 7 people with no restriction: . The answer is about 2.9%, roughly 1 chance in 35. So if a company’s “random” schedule happened to put all four women first, that would be surprising, which is the kind of reasoning hypothesis tests formalise later in the course.

5Permutations

Definition Permutations

A subset of distinct elements from a given set arranged in a specific order is called a permutation.

The number of objects in the subset is the length of the permutation.

If we select objects from a set of objects, how many different permutations can we make?

Example

You have 3 movies on DVD, Star trek, Star wars, and Stargate.

You want to choose 2 of the 3 movies to watch and the order in which you watch them matters.

How many ways can you choose 2 of the 3 movies to watch?

Possibilities:

ST, SW
ST, SG
SW, ST
SW, SG
SG, ST
SG, SW

These are the 6 permutations of length 2 we can make from our set of 3 objects.

Notation: denotes the number of permutations of length that can be made from a set of objects.

✎ Explanation (added)

ST = Star Trek, SW = Star Wars, SG = Stargate. Because order matters, “ST, SW” (Star Trek first) and “SW, ST” (Star Wars first) are two different permutations even though they contain the same two movies. Keep an eye on those pairs: they are exactly what combinations will merge.

Watch the order of the subscripts: this course (following Devore) writes with the length first. Many other books and the TI-84 write with first.

Textbook · Devore — permutation: Definition in §2.3, p. 69, with the same notation Pk,n.

6Combinations

Definition Combinations

These are very similar to permutations, but now the order in which we arrange the objects does not matter.

To find the number of combinations of length we can make from a set of objects, start with the list of all permutations of length you can make and then group equivalent combinations together.

✎ Explanation (added)

If the question were “which 2 of the 3 movies will you watch this weekend?” with no interest in the order, then {ST, SW} is one choice, however you list it. The 6 ordered lists collapse into 3 unordered choices: 6 ÷ 2 = 3. The 2 is the number of ways to order two movies.

Textbook · Devore — combinations: §2.3, pp. 70–71. Devore writes the count as the binomial coefficient “n choose k” and also as Ck,n.

Since the number of ways you can arrange objects is , each group of equivalent combinations will have permutations in it.

Since the number of combinations of length that can be made from the objects is just the number of groups we make and each group has permutations in it, the number of combinations of length that can be made from distinct objects is:

← Number of groups

How to choose between the two: ask “if I rearranged my selection, would it count as a different outcome?” Yes (a schedule, a ranking, a password, president and vice-president): permutation. No (a committee, a hand of cards, lottery numbers): combination.

Textbook · Devore — “n choose k” = Pk,n/k! = n!/(k!(n − k)!): Proposition in §2.3, p. 71, argued the same way.

7Example: 5-card hands with exactly one pair

Example

How many 5 card hands can be selected from a standard deck of 52 playing cards that have exactly one pair?

  • ↑ choose the denomination for the pair
  • ↑ choose 2 of the 4 cards of this denomination
  • ↖ choose the denominations of the other 3 cards
  • (under one brace) — choose the suit for the other three cards
Typed note included in the PDF Example: 5-Card Hands with Exactly One Pair

How many 5-card hands can be selected from a standard deck of 52 playing cards that have exactly one pair?

FactorMeaning
choose the denomination for the pair
choose 2 of the 4 cards of that denomination
choose the denominations of the other 3 cards
choose the suit for each of the other three cards
✎ Explanation (added)

A standard deck has 13 denominations (A, 2, …, 10, J, Q, K) in each of 4 suits. The method is the multiplication rule again: build the hand through a sequence of activities, each counted with a combination because order within a hand does not matter.

The values: ; ; ; and three times, . Product: .

Why and not : the other three cards must have three different denominations, all different from the pair’s (12 denominations remain). Otherwise the hand could become two pairs, three of a kind or a full house, which are not “exactly one pair”. Choosing the three denominations together with one , instead of , also avoids counting the same hand in several orders.

As a probability: there are possible hands, so .

8Conditional probability

Conditional Probability

If event has occurred, what is the probability event has also occurred?

Let’s do this in the classical case for now.

If one of the outcomes in has occurred, what is the probability the outcome that occurred is also in ?

Textbook · Devore — §2.4 Conditional Probability starts on p. 75. Example 2.24 (pp. 75–76) and Figure 2.8 motivate the definition by restricting attention to the outcomes in the given event.

If one of the outcomes in occurred, we can restrict the sample space to just those outcomes in .

If also occurred, one of the outcomes in occurred.

( in the pictured example)

✱ Formula for Conditional Probability:

← Probability of the intersection ← divided by the probability of the given event.

This works in the nonclassical case as well.

The second line divides top and bottom by , which does not change the fraction () but turns the two counts into probabilities. That form no longer mentions counting, which is why it can be used as the definition even when outcomes are not equally likely. It needs .

What a typical exam question looks like
  • A “how many ways” question solved by writing out a sequence of activities and multiplying, with a restriction such as “no repeated digits” or “the first digit cannot be 0 or 1”.
  • An arrangement with a condition (all the women before the men), followed by “if all orders are equally likely, what is the probability?”, answered as favourable count over total count.
  • Decide between a permutation and a combination, state why (does order matter?), and evaluate or .
  • Explain or derive by grouping permutations.
  • A card-hand count built from several “choose” factors, where you must say what each factor chooses (for example, exactly one pair).
  • Given a Venn diagram or the values of and : find with the formula.
